grounded_claims.sentence: The ability to maintain correct posture alignment is a crucial indicator of both musculoskeletal health and central nervous system integrity, with impairment often associated with an underlying pathological condition [1], [2], [3], [4].

It is impossible to have good posture associated with poor balance, yet it is possible to achieve good balance despite poor posture through compensatory strategies [9].

Therefore, information obtained from direct postural angle measurements can be particularly relevant for early detection of abnormalities in disease progression or for tracking changes resulting from rehabilitative treatments [10].

Although quantitative analysis of these angular measurements can be challenging and less commonly practiced in routine clinical practice [11], several techniques have been employed in the past decades for accurately assessing postural alterations.

Among these techniques, one of the most popular in the literature is photographic postural assessment, a method based on angular measurements obtained by identifying specific body landmarks on photographic images [9], [10], [11], [12], [13].
This technique has established itself as an alternative to more invasive radiography-based methods for measuring certain spinal deformities [14], [15].
However, it is poorly standardized, with significant challenges related to the choice of reference points, analysis software, and camera position/resolution [16].
Other techniques based on direct goniometer measurements are often lengthy and impractical for routine use [11], [17].
By using marker configurations placed on the body according to standardized biomechanical models, they limit the variability in the selection of reference points [18], [19].
In recent years, there has been growing interest in new digital technologies for movement analysis, including wearable sensors and low-cost visionbased approaches [20], [21], [22], [23], [24].

A major push in this direction came from RGB-D cameras, a standard RGB camera enhanced by robust depth estimation, which made 3D motion analysis more accessible and enabled the development of highly accurate markerless solutions for movement, posture, and balance control [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30], [31].
State-of-the-art analysis reveals that HPE frameworks are rapidly gaining popularity across various sectors, including the medical field [32], [33], [34], [35], [36], [37].
However, significant challenges remain [38], including the need for rigorous validation versus gold standard references to evaluate accuracy and robustness for clinical applications.

Among the most promising next-generation HPE frameworks is Google MediaPipe Pose (MP) [39], an open-source algorithm that tracks 33 body landmarks from RGB-only sources (i.e., images or videos), effectively providing 2D (image coordinates) and 3D (world coordinates) skeletal models.

Compared to other HPE frameworks, such as Open- Pose [40] and custom multi-level architectures [20], the main strength of MP relies on its highly optimized and lightweight pipeline, which enables real-time detection and tracking.

For example, MP performance was evaluated for specific repetitive arm and leg movements [41] and for detecting upper limb impairments in individuals with spinal cord injuries [42], finding good correlations between the estimated metrics and impairment severity, respectively.
In gait analysis, MP has demonstrated low mean absolute errors and performance comparable to those of optoelectronic systems [43], [44].

Other applications of MP include detecting sex-based differences in static posture from photographs using 2D models [45], measuring height in infants from XY coordinates [46], and evaluating movement metrics in physical exercises with multi-view solutions using 2D models [47].
MATERIALS AND METHODS This study analyzed a subset of experimental trials collected within the REHOME project [48].

The REHOME project developed a portable motion-capture system based on a single RGB-D camera for the quantitative evaluation of motion skills and movement dysfunction across various domains, including gait, posture, and upper/lower limb mobility on healthy and pathological subjects [49].
This approach avoids the potential discomfort associated with wearing only the underwear [50], which is a common requirement for marker-based motion capture systems.

This choice was supported by several studies demonstrating superior depth sensor performance [51], [52], [53] and body tracking capabilities [54], [55], [56] compared with both previous Kinect models and other less expensive RGB-D cameras.
The OPTO and AK acquisitions were performed separately to prevent the retroreflective markers from interfering with the AK depth estimation and to ensure robust body tracking [57], [58].

The OPTO system (VICON, Oxford Metrics Ltd., Oxford, United Kingdom; sampling rate: 100 Hz) comprised six infrared cameras operating at 100 Hz and tracking markers within a calibrated working volume of 5 × 2 × 2 m^{3}).
Its accuracy is specified as <0.3 mm RMS for static measurements and <1 mm for dynamic acquisitions.

For the assessment, an ad hoc set of 24 spherical retroreflective markers (15 mm diameter) was attached to the participant’s body with biocompatible double-sided adhesive tape, following the complete Plug-In Gait biomechanical model [59],

This subset included markers positioned on the head (frontal), shoulders (acromion), hips (anterior superior iliac spine), knees (lateral epicondyle), and ankles (lateral malleolus), which are particularly important in posture, gait, and balance clinical assessments [61].
The AK system, configured as described in [49], employed a proprietary body-tracking algorithm (Azure Kinect Body Tracking SDK v1.1.0) to estimate a 3D skeletal model with 33 joints in real time.

Wrong executions and overexertion while doing at-home exercises might lead to an inefficient training or even worse, serious injuries [3].

The measurement setup consisted of two cameras (C1 and C2) positioned perpendicular to one another, recording an area of approximately 5 × 5 meters, and the MTw Awinda MoCap system by Movella1, which has proven to be a reliable and accurate system to track human movement [5] and has been previously used in exercise-related movement analysis [2].
The MoCap suit captured data with 60 Hz, which was downsampled to match the 30 Hz of the cameras.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. The framework is a deep learning model based on EfficientPose and T-GCN, specifically designed for efficient real-time action pose estimation in sports events. The model takes a video sequence [x1, x2, . . . , xt ] as input, where each video frame is first processed through the EfficientPose backbone network for feature extraction. The extracted features are then passed through a pose regression module to obtain keypoint information. The resulting keypoints, along with the temporal sequence data, are fed into the T-GCN network for temporal modeling. In this way, the model is capable of accurately estimating human poses.

FIGURE 3. The figure presents a runtime performance comparison of various 3D pose estimation models, including HRNet (3D), PoseResNet (3D), OpenPose (3D), AlphaPose (3D), ST-GCN (3D), and SufficientPose + T-GCN (Ours). The x-axis represents the number of people in the input data, ranging from 2 to 10, while the y-axis indicates the runtime in milliseconds (ms). The results demonstrate that OpenPose consistently exhibits the highest runtime, while SufficientPose + T-GCN achieves the lowest runtime across all scenarios, underscoring its efficiency. The other models display runtime performance with varying linear growth trends as the number of people increases, with HRNet and PoseResNet showing relatively moderate increases.

In the research on action pose estimation and real-time feedback systems, OpenPose [4] can accurately detect joint locations from a single image, making it suitable for processing planar information in images.

To address this limitation, DensePose [5] is capable of better capturing depth information and analyzing dynamic scene details but still faces challenges in low-resolution images or multi-person scenarios, where the network must handle large amounts of computation, leading to poor realtime performance.
In response to the limitations of these methods, this paper focuses on the latest advancements in EfficientPose [6].
EfficientPose introduces a CNN [7], [8] based feature extraction method and a highly efficient and accurate 3D pose estimation approach.
Compared to traditional pose estimation methods, EfficientPose provides more accurate 3D pose predictions [9], [10] while reducing computational overhead, making it ideal for real-time applications.

In response, this study focuses on T-GCN (Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks) [12].
T-GCN combines the advantages of GCN [13] and RNN [14], capturing both temporal changes and spatial dependencies.

Human Activity Recognition (HAR) aims to identify human activities based on the full execution of actions captured in videos, serving as a core task in video understand­ ing [1].
For instance, activity recognition algorithms power visual surveillance systems that assist in capturing criminals through video analysis, reducing the risks of criminal activities [2].
Video retrieval enables users to search for videos matching textual descriptions (e.g., titles or keywords) on the internet [3].
Additionally, virtual reality (VR) technologies based on depth sensor data have attracted a large audience across all age groups in the gaming industry [4].

Among these, skelecton-based activity recognition has gained increasing attention in recent years due to advances in human pose estimation algorithms [5,6] and the robustness of skelecton data, which captures human activity information without being influenced by noisy backgrounds or variations in lighting [7].

Early approaches treated skeletal trajectories as either coordinate vector sequences or grid-like struc­ tures, inputting them into Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [8] or Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) [9].
However, RNNs and ConvNets are inherently designed for regular Euclidean data, and due to the irregular nature of skelecton data, these methods fail to fully exploit the affinities among nodes [8].
Graph Convo­ lutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) [10], which excel in handling irregular data, have thus been introduced for modeling skelecton data.
Although existing GCNN-based methods have demonstrated notable performance, most approaches alternate spatial graph convolutions and temporal graph convolu­ tions independently [11–14].
[15] proposed a dataset-independent and translation-scale-invariant mapping method, converting 3D skelecton data into color images with guaranteed invariance in scale.
[16] introduced a dual-stream ConvNet model that considers both node and bone features, employing asymmetric convolution blocks to mitigate deformation effects in skelecton trajectories.
[31] defined custom distance features based on skelecton data, mapping them into textured color images and training the model with AlexNet.
[32] proposed Joint Trajectory Maps (JTMs), which encode spatiotemporal node trajectory information as three texture images from front, side, and top views for activity recognition.

However, ConvNet-based methods in skelecton activity recognition often simplify skelecton information into image representations, limiting feature learning to adjacent nodes within a convolution kernel [33].

grounded_claims.sentence: The ability to maintain correct posture alignment is a crucial indicator of both musculoskeletal health and central nervous system integrity, with impairment often associated with an underlying pathological condition [1], [2], [3], [4].

It is impossible to have good posture associated with poor balance, yet it is possible to achieve good balance despite poor posture through compensatory strategies [9].

Therefore, information obtained from direct postural angle measurements can be particularly relevant for early detection of abnormalities in disease progression or for tracking changes resulting from rehabilitative treatments [10].

Although quantitative analysis of these angular measurements can be challenging and less commonly practiced in routine clinical practice [11], several techniques have been employed in the past decades for accurately assessing postural alterations.

Among these techniques, one of the most popular in the literature is photographic postural assessment, a method based on angular measurements obtained by identifying specific body landmarks on photographic images [9], [10], [11], [12], [13].
This technique has established itself as an alternative to more invasive radiography-based methods for measuring certain spinal deformities [14], [15].
However, it is poorly standardized, with significant challenges related to the choice of reference points, analysis software, and camera position/resolution [16].
Other techniques based on direct goniometer measurements are often lengthy and impractical for routine use [11], [17].
By using marker configurations placed on the body according to standardized biomechanical models, they limit the variability in the selection of reference points [18], [19].
In recent years, there has been growing interest in new digital technologies for movement analysis, including wearable sensors and low-cost visionbased approaches [20], [21], [22], [23], [24].

A major push in this direction came from RGB-D cameras, a standard RGB camera enhanced by robust depth estimation, which made 3D motion analysis more accessible and enabled the development of highly accurate markerless solutions for movement, posture, and balance control [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30], [31].
State-of-the-art analysis reveals that HPE frameworks are rapidly gaining popularity across various sectors, including the medical field [32], [33], [34], [35], [36], [37].
However, significant challenges remain [38], including the need for rigorous validation versus gold standard references to evaluate accuracy and robustness for clinical applications.

Among the most promising next-generation HPE frameworks is Google MediaPipe Pose (MP) [39], an open-source algorithm that tracks 33 body landmarks from RGB-only sources (i.e., images or videos), effectively providing 2D (image coordinates) and 3D (world coordinates) skeletal models.

Compared to other HPE frameworks, such as Open- Pose [40] and custom multi-level architectures [20], the main strength of MP relies on its highly optimized and lightweight pipeline, which enables real-time detection and tracking.

For example, MP performance was evaluated for specific repetitive arm and leg movements [41] and for detecting upper limb impairments in individuals with spinal cord injuries [42], finding good correlations between the estimated metrics and impairment severity, respectively.
In gait analysis, MP has demonstrated low mean absolute errors and performance comparable to those of optoelectronic systems [43], [44].

Other applications of MP include detecting sex-based differences in static posture from photographs using 2D models [45], measuring height in infants from XY coordinates [46], and evaluating movement metrics in physical exercises with multi-view solutions using 2D models [47].
MATERIALS AND METHODS This study analyzed a subset of experimental trials collected within the REHOME project [48].

The REHOME project developed a portable motion-capture system based on a single RGB-D camera for the quantitative evaluation of motion skills and movement dysfunction across various domains, including gait, posture, and upper/lower limb mobility on healthy and pathological subjects [49].
This approach avoids the potential discomfort associated with wearing only the underwear [50], which is a common requirement for marker-based motion capture systems.

This choice was supported by several studies demonstrating superior depth sensor performance [51], [52], [53] and body tracking capabilities [54], [55], [56] compared with both previous Kinect models and other less expensive RGB-D cameras.
The OPTO and AK acquisitions were performed separately to prevent the retroreflective markers from interfering with the AK depth estimation and to ensure robust body tracking [57], [58].

The OPTO system (VICON, Oxford Metrics Ltd., Oxford, United Kingdom; sampling rate: 100 Hz) comprised six infrared cameras operating at 100 Hz and tracking markers within a calibrated working volume of 5 × 2 × 2 m^{3}).
Its accuracy is specified as <0.3 mm RMS for static measurements and <1 mm for dynamic acquisitions.

For the assessment, an ad hoc set of 24 spherical retroreflective markers (15 mm diameter) was attached to the participant’s body with biocompatible double-sided adhesive tape, following the complete Plug-In Gait biomechanical model [59],

This subset included markers positioned on the head (frontal), shoulders (acromion), hips (anterior superior iliac spine), knees (lateral epicondyle), and ankles (lateral malleolus), which are particularly important in posture, gait, and balance clinical assessments [61].
The AK system, configured as described in [49], employed a proprietary body-tracking algorithm (Azure Kinect Body Tracking SDK v1.1.0) to estimate a 3D skeletal model with 33 joints in real time.

The AK system outputs a JSON file containing the 3D coordinates for the 33joint skeletal model, the recorded video (MP4, 640 × 360px, 30 fps, 40 s), and the intrinsic parameters of the camera for both the color and depth sensors.

A key advantage of MP is that it operates on RGB-only video input [39], thereby eliminating the hardware complexity associated with RGB-D sensors, while maintaining real-time performance through optimized neural network architectures.

Because of this additional property, this model is often considered a 2.5D model, in contrast to purely 2D models from other frameworks, such as OpenPose [40].

First, we established a common temporal base by resampling all signals (i.e., trajectories) to 50 Hz, which involved downsampling the OPTO marker trajectories from their original 100 Hz) and upsampling the AK joint and MP landmark trajectories from their original 30 fps.
Subsequently, we applied a fourth-order Butterworth low-pass filter with a 10 Hz cutoff frequency to suppress high-frequency noise while preserving the physiological components of the movement.

Five categories (horizontal, vertical, sagittal, joint, and length metrics) were considered to comprehensively quantify postural features, thus approximating traditional clinical metrics of posture derived from observational, goniometric, photographic, or stereophotogrammetric techniques [17], [63], [64].

Reliability was assessed via the Standard Error of Measurement (SEM), which indicates the typical error in a single observation, and the Minimal Detectable Change (MDC95), which represents the smallest change that can be considered real with 95% confidence.

Agreement was evaluated using the Bland-Altman analysis to compute the measurement bias (systematic error between models) and the 95% Limits of Agreement (LOA), which defines the precision range for individual measurements.

In [26], the authors reported an ICC > 0.90 for many AK joint trajectories in postural tasks.
In [28], postural measures were input into machine learning models, achieving consistent classification (90% accuracy) with clinical scores.
The authors in [31] and [66] obtained a high level of agreement (accuracy > 90%) in assessing gait profiles from the parameters estimated using AK.
High agreements and correlations were also reported in [56] and [67] for most spatio-temporal parameters.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. The framework is a deep learning model based on EfficientPose and T-GCN, specifically designed for efficient real-time action pose estimation in sports events. The model takes a video sequence [x1, x2, . . . , xt ] as input, where each video frame is first processed through the EfficientPose backbone network for feature extraction. The extracted features are then passed through a pose regression module to obtain keypoint information. The resulting keypoints, along with the temporal sequence data, are fed into the T-GCN network for temporal modeling. In this way, the model is capable of accurately estimating human poses.

FIGURE 3. The figure presents a runtime performance comparison of various 3D pose estimation models, including HRNet (3D), PoseResNet (3D), OpenPose (3D), AlphaPose (3D), ST-GCN (3D), and SufficientPose + T-GCN (Ours). The x-axis represents the number of people in the input data, ranging from 2 to 10, while the y-axis indicates the runtime in milliseconds (ms). The results demonstrate that OpenPose consistently exhibits the highest runtime, while SufficientPose + T-GCN achieves the lowest runtime across all scenarios, underscoring its efficiency. The other models display runtime performance with varying linear growth trends as the number of people increases, with HRNet and PoseResNet showing relatively moderate increases.

Extensive experiments on NTU‐RGB + D, NTU‐RGB + D 120, and Toyota Smarthome demonstrate ASTM‐Net’s superiority: it outperforms DualHead‐Net‐ALLs by 0.31% on NTU‐RGB + D X‐Sub and surpasses SkateFormer by 2.22% on Toyota Smarthome Cross‐Subject; it reduces parameters by 51.9% and FLOPs by 49.7% compared to MST‐GCNN‐ALLs while improving accuracy by 0.82%; and under 30% random node occlusion, it achieves 86.94% accuracy—3.49% higher than CBAM‐STGCN.
Human Activity Recognition (HAR) aims to identify human activities based on the full execution of actions captured in videos, serving as a core task in video understand­ ing [1].
For instance, activity recognition algorithms power visual surveillance systems that assist in capturing criminals through video analysis, reducing the risks of criminal activities [2].
Video retrieval enables users to search for videos matching textual descriptions (e.g., titles or keywords) on the internet [3].
Additionally, virtual reality (VR) technologies based on depth sensor data have attracted a large audience across all age groups in the gaming industry [4].

Among these, skelecton-based activity recognition has gained increasing attention in recent years due to advances in human pose estimation algorithms [5,6] and the robustness of skelecton data, which captures human activity information without being influenced by noisy backgrounds or variations in lighting [7].

Early approaches treated skeletal trajectories as either coordinate vector sequences or grid-like struc­ tures, inputting them into Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [8] or Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) [9].
However, RNNs and ConvNets are inherently designed for regular Euclidean data, and due to the irregular nature of skelecton data, these methods fail to fully exploit the affinities among nodes [8].
Graph Convo­ lutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) [10], which excel in handling irregular data, have thus been introduced for modeling skelecton data.
Although existing GCNN-based methods have demonstrated notable performance, most approaches alternate spatial graph convolutions and temporal graph convolu­ tions independently [11–14].
